tool.name: collections
tool.tagline: Specialised containers: Counter, defaultdict, deque, namedtuple and more
tool.description: The collections module adds high-performance container types to Python's built-in list, dict, set and tuple: Counter for tallies, defaultdict for grouping, deque for queues, namedtuple for lightweight records, OrderedDict and ChainMap for ordering and layering. Its companion collections.abc defines the abstract interfaces of all containers. Using the right container makes code shorter and often much faster.

glossary.def: A kind of dict from Python's collections module that counts how many times each item appears. Items it hasn't seen count as 0.
A kind of dict from Python's collections module that creates a starting value (such as an empty list) the first time you use a key that isn't there yet.
A function whose job is to make and give back a new value. A defaultdict calls one, such as list, to create the value for a missing key.
Pronounced "deck": a list-like container from Python's collections module that adds and removes items quickly at both its front and its back.
A short way to say how an operation's time grows with the amount of data n: O(1) stays the same however much data there is, O(n) grows in step with it.
A set in which an item can appear more than once, like a bag of letter tiles with three e's. A Counter works as one.
In programming, a set of points (nodes) joined by lines (edges), like towns joined by roads or people joined by friendships.
A way to explore a graph that visits everything one step away from the start, then everything two steps away, and so on, so it finds the shortest route first.
The last few items of a sequence (say the last 3 numbers), moved along one item at a time, as in a moving average.
Taking turns in a fixed cycle: serve A, then B, then C, then A again, so everyone gets a fair share.
A dict from Python's collections module with extra operations for changing the order of its keys, such as moving a key to the end.
A "least recently used" cache: a store of limited size that, when full, throws out the item nobody has used for the longest time.
A view from Python's collections module that searches several dicts in order, as if they were one, without copying them.
Short for abstract base class: a class that only describes which methods a kind of object must have, for other classes to build on.
A method an abstract base class names but doesn't write; every class that builds on it must supply its own version before it can be used.
A class in Python's collections module, written in plain Python, that wraps a real dict so your own versions of its methods are always used.
A chain of small memory blocks where each block holds a pointer to the next one (and, if doubly linked, the previous one), so adding at either end is cheap.

concepts.name: Counting with Counter
concepts.summary: Tally items with Counter and get the most common ones.
concepts.why: Counting words, events, errors or votes is one of the most common data tasks.
concepts.body:
Counting how often things appear is a classic dict job. The dictionaries lesson did it by hand: `counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1`. The `collections` module, part of Python's standard library, has a ready-made tool for exactly this.

A **Counter** is a special kind of dict whose values are counts. Give it a list, or anything else a `for` loop can go through, and it counts each item:

```python
from collections import Counter
words = Counter(text.split())
```

The items become the keys, so like any dict keys they must be immutable: strings, numbers or tuples.

A Counter works like a normal dict, with a few conveniences:

- Missing items count as **0** instead of stopping with `KeyError`: `words["zebra"]` is `0`. Reading doesn't add the key.
- `c.most_common(3)` gives the three most frequent `(item, count)` pairs, highest first; ties keep the order items were first seen. Without a number it gives all items.
- `c.update(more_items)` adds more counts; `c[item] += 1` works directly too.
- `c.total()` (Python 3.10 and later) adds up all the counts.

You can also start a Counter from a dict of counts or from keyword arguments: `Counter({"a": 2})`, `Counter(a=2, b=1)`.

Counting a string counts its **characters**, a common surprise: `Counter("hello")` has `l: 2`. Split the text first if you want words.

A Counter replaces the hand-written counting loop. Its counting happens inside Python's own fast built-in code, so it is also quicker on large amounts of data.
concepts.code:
from collections import Counter

text = "the cat and the hat and the bat"
words = Counter(text.split())
print(words["the"], words["dog"])   # 3 0
print(words.most_common(2))         # [('the', 3), ('and', 2)]
print(words.total())                # 8

words.update(["cat", "cat"])
words["hat"] += 1
print(words["cat"], words["hat"])   # 3 2

print(Counter("hello"))             # Counter({'l': 2, 'h': 1, 'e': 1, 'o': 1})
status = Counter([200, 404, 200, 500, 200])
print(status.most_common(1)[0])     # (200, 3)
takeaways: `Counter(iterable)` tallies items; missing keys count as 0
`most_common(n)` returns the top items with counts
Counting a string counts characters, not words
pitfalls: Passing a sentence string directly to Counter when you meant to count words.

quiz.q: c = Counter(['a', 'b', 'a']). What does c['z'] return, and does 'z' get added?
quiz.explain: Counter returns 0 for missing items without inserting them.

concepts.name: Grouping with defaultdict
concepts.summary: Let missing keys get an automatic default value, the idiomatic way to group items into lists or sets.
concepts.why: Grouping things by a key is everywhere: orders by customer, files by type, pupils by school year.
concepts.body:
Grouping is the other classic dict job: put each file name in a list under its ending (`.py`, `.md`), each order under its customer. With a plain dict you must first check whether the key exists and, if not, store an empty list. A **defaultdict** does that check for you.

When you use a key that isn't there yet, a defaultdict calls a **factory function**, a function whose job is to make a new value, and stores what it gives back:

```python
from collections import defaultdict
by_ext = defaultdict(list)
by_ext[".py"].append("app.py")   # empty list created automatically
```

You pass the function itself, without brackets: `list`, not `list()`. Written without brackets, a function's name just refers to the function; the defaultdict calls it later, once per new key. Common choices:

- `defaultdict(list)` groups items into lists (`list()` gives `[]`).
- `defaultdict(set)` groups items without repeats.
- `defaultdict(int)` counts, because `int()` gives 0 (though `Counter` is usually nicer).

For any other starting value, write a **lambda**: a tiny function with no name, written in place. `defaultdict(lambda: "n/a")` makes every missing key start as `"n/a"`.

Watch out: any `d[key]` creates the entry, even if you only meant to read. That can quietly grow the dict. To check without creating anything, use `key in d` or `d.get(key)`; `get` never calls the factory.

Older code writes `d.setdefault(key, []).append(x)`, which gives back the existing value or stores and gives back `[]`. A defaultdict says the same thing more clearly, and doesn't build an unused empty list on every call.

A defaultdict prints as `defaultdict(<class 'list'>, {...})`. Turn it back into an ordinary dict with `dict(d)` before handing it to other code, so a missing key there raises `KeyError` as people expect instead of silently being added.
concepts.code:
from collections import defaultdict

files = ["app.py", "README.md", "test_app.py", "setup.cfg", "notes.md"]
by_ext = defaultdict(list)
for name in files:
    by_ext[name.rsplit(".", 1)[-1]].append(name)   # text after the last "."
print(dict(by_ext))
# {'py': ['app.py', 'test_app.py'], 'md': ['README.md', 'notes.md'], 'cfg': ['setup.cfg']}

friends = defaultdict(set)          # who knows whom
for a, b in [("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("B", "C")]:
    friends[a].add(b)
    friends[b].add(a)
print(sorted(friends["C"]))         # ['A', 'B']

print(friends.get("Z"))             # None: get doesn't add Z
print(friends["Z"], "Z" in friends) # set() True: [] does add Z
takeaways: `defaultdict(factory)` creates missing values by calling the factory
Pass the factory uncalled: `list`, not `list()`
`d[key]` inserts on read; use `in` or `get` to check without inserting
pitfalls: Writing `defaultdict([])`; the argument must be a function such as `list`, not a value.

quiz.q: d = defaultdict(int); d['a'] += 1; x = d['b']. What is len(d)?
quiz.explain: Reading d['b'] also inserts the default 0, so both keys exist.

concepts.name: Records with namedtuple
concepts.summary: Create lightweight, unchangeable records whose parts can be read by name as well as by position.
concepts.why: Named parts make tuples returned from functions or read from CSV files say what they mean: `p.x` instead of `p[0]`.
concepts.body:
The tuples lesson warned that `row[3]` doesn't say what position 3 means. `namedtuple` fixes that: it creates a new kind of tuple whose positions also have names, called **fields**:

```python
from collections import namedtuple
Point = namedtuple("Point", ["x", "y"])
p = Point(3, 4)
p.x, p[1]        # 3, 4
```

`Point` is now a maker of points, a bit like `list` makes lists. Each point it makes is a **named tuple**.

Because it really is a tuple, a named tuple can't be changed, can be unpacked (`x, y = p`), compares equal to a plain tuple with the same values, and can be a dict key if its values can. It takes no more memory than a plain tuple. When printed it shows the field names, `Point(x=3, y=4)`, which makes output easy to read while hunting bugs.

A few extras (their names start with an underscore so they can't clash with your field names):

- `p._replace(x=10)` gives a copy with some fields changed.
- `p._asdict()` gives a dict of the fields.
- `Point._fields` lists the field names; `Point._make(values)` builds one from a list, handy for the lines of a CSV file.
- `namedtuple("P", "x y", defaults=[0])` gives default values to the last fields.

Field names can be given as a list or as one string separated by spaces or commas. With `rename=True`, names that aren't allowed (such as `class` or `def`, words Python reserves for itself) are replaced by `_0`, `_1` and so on.

Python has two relatives you'll meet later: `typing.NamedTuple`, another way to write the same thing that also records each field's type, and `dataclasses`, for records whose fields need to change.
concepts.code:
import csv
import io
from collections import namedtuple

Point = namedtuple("Point", "x y")
p = Point(3, 4)
print(p)                     # Point(x=3, y=4)
print(p.x + p[1])            # 7
x, y = p
print(p._replace(y=0))       # Point(x=3, y=0)
print(p._asdict())           # {'x': 3, 'y': 4}

rows = io.StringIO("name,qty\napple,3\npear,5\n")   # text that acts like a file
reader = csv.reader(rows)
Item = namedtuple("Item", next(reader))   # field names from the header line
items = [Item._make(r) for r in reader]
print(items[1].name, items[1].qty)   # pear 5

Config = namedtuple("Config", "host port debug", defaults=[8000, False])
print(Config("localhost"))   # Config(host='localhost', port=8000, debug=False)
takeaways: namedtuple adds field names to a lightweight, unchangeable tuple
`_replace`, `_asdict`, `_fields` and `_make` cover common needs
For records whose fields must change, use dataclasses instead
pitfalls: Trying `p.x = 5`; namedtuples are immutable, so use `_replace`.

quiz.q: Point = namedtuple('Point', 'x y'). What does Point(1, 2) == (1, 2) return?
options: It depends on the field names
True, because a namedtuple is a tuple
quiz.explain: namedtuple instances are tuples and compare equal to plain tuples with the same values.

concepts.name: Fast queues with deque
concepts.summary: Use deque to add and remove items quickly at both ends, and maxlen to keep only the last N items.
concepts.why: Waiting lines of tasks, undo history and 'keep the last N items' all need quick adding and removing at both ends.
concepts.body:
The lists lesson showed that a list is quick at its end but slow at its front: `lst.pop(0)` and `lst.insert(0, x)` have to shift every other item along by one place. On a list of a million items, that's a million moves each time.

Programmers describe this with **Big-O notation**. O(1) means an operation takes the same time however many items there are. O(n) means its time grows in step with the number of items, n. Removing from the front of a list is O(n).

A **deque** (said "deck", short for double-ended queue) is quick, O(1), at **both** ends:

- `append(x)` and `appendleft(x)`
- `pop()` and `popleft()`
- `extend(items)` and `extendleft(items)` (which adds them in reverse order)

That makes it the right tool for a **queue**: a waiting line where the first item in is the first out, like people at a shop counter. `append` joins the back of the line; `popleft` serves the front.

Give a deque a **maxlen** and it never grows past that size: `deque(maxlen=3)` keeps only the last three items, dropping one from the opposite end each time you add a new one. It's ideal for "the last 100 lines a program printed" or the latest few readings.

A deque supports `len`, `for` loops, `in`, positions such as `d[0]` and `d[-1]`, and `clear()`. Positions near the ends are quick, but reaching the middle is O(n), and you can't cut out a section like `d[1:3]`. If you mostly read items by position, stay with a list.

Popping from an empty deque raises `IndexError`; check `if d:` first.

Later you'll write programs that do several things at once using **threads**. To pass work between threads, use `queue.Queue`, which can wait until an item arrives.
concepts.code:
from collections import deque

tasks = deque(["a", "b"])
tasks.append("c")              # join the back of the line
tasks.appendleft("urgent")     # jump the line
print(tasks.popleft())         # urgent
print(list(tasks))             # ['a', 'b', 'c']

recent = deque(maxlen=3)
for line in ["l1", "l2", "l3", "l4", "l5"]:
    recent.append(line)
print(list(recent))            # ['l3', 'l4', 'l5']
print(recent[0], recent[-1])   # l3 l5

d = deque()
d.extendleft([1, 2, 3])
print(d)                       # deque([3, 2, 1])
takeaways: deque adds and removes at both ends in O(1)
`maxlen` keeps only the most recent N items
To pass work between threads, use `queue.Queue`
pitfalls: Using `list.pop(0)` as a queue on large lists, which is O(n) per pop.

quiz.q: d = deque([1, 2, 3], maxlen=3); d.appendleft(0). What is d?
quiz.explain: Appending on the left of a full bounded deque discards an item from the right end.

concepts.name: Counter arithmetic and multisets
concepts.summary: Combine and compare Counters with +, -, &, |, subtract and comparison operators, treating them as multisets.
concepts.why: Comparing inventories, finding differences between word frequencies or checking anagrams all become one-liners.
concepts.body:
A Counter doubles as a **multiset**: a set where an item can appear several times, like a bag of letter tiles with three e's. You can do arithmetic between Counters:

- `a + b` adds counts.
- `a - b` subtracts counts and **drops zero and negative results**.
- `a & b` (intersection) keeps the smaller of each count.
- `a | b` (union) keeps the larger of each count.
- A lone `+` in front, `+a`, removes zero and negative entries; `-a` keeps only the negative counts, turned positive.

The method `a.subtract(b)` is different from `-`: it changes `a` itself and **keeps** negative and zero counts, which is what you want for balances like stock minus orders.

Since Python 3.10, Counters can also be **compared** as multisets: `a <= b` is true if every count in `a` is at most the count in `b`, with missing items counting as zero. That gives a neat "can I spell this word with these tiles?" check: `Counter(word) <= Counter(tiles)`. Equality also treats missing and zero counts as the same.

`c.elements()` goes the other way: it hands out each item repeated by its count (skipping counts below one). It gives the items one at a time, so wrap it in `list()` or `sorted()` to see them all.

These operations take time in step with the number of different items. They ignore order, so use them for questions about "how many", not "in what order".
concepts.code:
from collections import Counter

stock = Counter(apple=5, pear=2, kiwi=1)
order = Counter(apple=3, pear=4)

print(stock - order)            # Counter({'apple': 2, 'kiwi': 1})
balance = stock.copy()
balance.subtract(order)
print(balance)                  # Counter({'apple': 2, 'kiwi': 1, 'pear': -2})
print(+balance)                 # Counter({'apple': 2, 'kiwi': 1})
print(stock & order)            # Counter({'apple': 3, 'pear': 2})
print(stock | order)            # Counter({'apple': 5, 'pear': 4, 'kiwi': 1})

def can_spell(word, tiles):
    return Counter(word) <= Counter(tiles)
print(can_spell("tea", "eatx"), can_spell("teat", "eatx"))  # True False
print(Counter("listen") == Counter("silent"))               # True
print(sorted(Counter(a=2, b=1).elements()))                 # ['a', 'a', 'b']
takeaways: `+ - & |` treat Counters as multisets; `-` drops non-positive counts
`subtract()` keeps negative counts for balances
Comparisons like `<=` (3.10+) test multiset inclusion
pitfalls: Using `a - b` to compute a balance and losing the items that went negative.

quiz.explain: The - operator discards results that are zero or negative.

concepts.name: deque patterns: windows, BFS, rotation
concepts.summary: Apply deque to breadth-first search, sliding windows, round-robin turns with rotate, and keeping the tail of a file.
concepts.why: These patterns show up constantly in interviews and in real code that walks networks of linked things or handles data arriving one item at a time.
concepts.body:
Four patterns cover most uses of deque beyond a plain queue.

**Breadth-first search.** A **graph** is a set of points (nodes) joined by lines (edges): towns and roads, or people and friendships. To find the shortest route between two nodes, put the start in a deque; then repeatedly `popleft` a node and `append` its neighbours you haven't seen yet. Because the queue serves first-in first-out, every node one step away is visited before any node two steps away. This is **breadth-first search** (BFS), and in a graph where every edge counts as one step it finds the shortest path.

**Sliding windows.** A `deque(maxlen=k)` holds the last k values of a series of numbers arriving one by one: a **sliding window**, for moving averages or "were the last 5 readings all high?". For the classic interview task "maximum of every window", a deque of positions kept in decreasing value order solves it in O(n) overall.

**Round robin.** `d.rotate(n)` moves every item n steps to the right (negative n moves left), wrapping round. Or pop an item from the left, give it one turn of work, and append it back on the right. That gives each task a fair turn in a fixed cycle, called **round robin**.

**Tail of a file.** `deque(open(path), maxlen=10)` reads through the file once and keeps only the last ten lines, using a small fixed amount of memory however big the file is.

Changing a deque while a `for` loop goes through it raises `RuntimeError`. Collect the changes separately, or loop with `while d:` and `popleft`.
takeaways: BFS uses a deque as a first-in first-out queue to visit nodes in order of distance
`deque(maxlen=k)` gives a sliding window or the tail of a file
`rotate(n)` shifts items in a cycle for round-robin turns
pitfalls: Doing BFS with `list.pop(0)`: each pop is O(n), so on a big graph the search slows down enormously.

quiz.q: Why does BFS with a deque find shortest paths in an unweighted graph?
options: FIFO order processes all nodes at distance k before any at distance k+1
quiz.explain: First-in-first-out order expands the search frontier level by level.

concepts.name: OrderedDict and LRU caches
concepts.summary: Know what OrderedDict still adds over insertion-ordered dicts: move_to_end, popitem(last=False) and order-sensitive equality.
concepts.why: Building a size-limited cache that throws out the least-used item is simplest with OrderedDict's extra operations.
concepts.body:
Since Python 3.7 a plain `dict` remembers the order keys were added, so you no longer need OrderedDict just for ordering. It is still useful for three extra abilities:

- `od.move_to_end(key)` moves a key to the end (or to the front with `last=False`), quickly.
- `od.popitem(last=False)` removes the **first**, oldest item; a plain `dict.popitem()` can only remove the last.
- Comparing two OrderedDicts with `==` checks the **order** too: `OrderedDict(a=1, b=2) != OrderedDict(b=2, a=1)`. Compared with a plain dict, order is ignored.

Those first two make it the classic building block for a cache. A **cache** keeps results you've already computed or fetched, so asking again is instant. Memory is limited, so a cache must throw something out when it's full. An **LRU cache** ("least recently used") throws out whatever nobody has used for the longest time.

With an OrderedDict that's two lines: on every use, `move_to_end(key)`, so the oldest-used key drifts to the front; when the cache is too big, `popitem(last=False)` removes that front key.

In everyday code, prefer plain dicts: they're faster and use less memory. To remember a function's results, Python's `functools.lru_cache` does all of this for you. Reach for OrderedDict when you need your own rules for what to throw out, or a cache that isn't tied to one function.

To reorder a plain dict, you have to rebuild it, for example `dict(sorted(d.items()))`.
concepts.code:
from collections import OrderedDict

class LRU:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.data, self.capacity = OrderedDict(), capacity
    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.data:
            return None
        self.data.move_to_end(key)          # mark as recently used
        return self.data[key]
    def put(self, key, value):
        self.data[key] = value
        self.data.move_to_end(key)
        if len(self.data) > self.capacity:
            self.data.popitem(last=False)   # evict least recently used

cache = LRU(2)
cache.put("a", 1); cache.put("b", 2)
cache.get("a")
cache.put("c", 3)                           # evicts "b"
print(list(cache.data))                     # ['a', 'c']

print(OrderedDict(a=1, b=2) == OrderedDict(b=2, a=1))   # False
print(OrderedDict(a=1, b=2) == dict(b=2, a=1))          # True
takeaways: Plain dicts keep insertion order; OrderedDict adds `move_to_end` and `popitem(last=False)`
OrderedDict equality checks order when comparing two OrderedDicts
It's the classic structure for a hand-made LRU cache
pitfalls: Using OrderedDict everywhere just for ordering, which plain dicts already provide.

quiz.q: Which operation does OrderedDict support efficiently that a plain dict does not?
options: Removing the oldest inserted item with popitem(last=False)
quiz.explain: Plain dict.popitem removes only the last item; OrderedDict can pop from either end.

concepts.name: Layered lookups with ChainMap
concepts.summary: Search several dicts as one with ChainMap, for layered settings and nested lookups.
concepts.why: Settings usually come in layers: built-in defaults, a settings file, environment variables, and options typed on the command line, each one winning over the layers below it.
concepts.body:
A **ChainMap** groups several dicts (or other mappings, things that look up values by key) into one view. A lookup searches them in order and returns the first hit:

```python
config = ChainMap(cli_args, env_vars, file_settings, defaults)
config["port"]   # from the first dict that has "port"
```

Nothing is copied: the ChainMap holds references to the dicts, so changes to them show through at once. That makes it cheaper and more "live" than merging them into a new dict with `{**defaults, **file, **env}`.

Environment variables are named settings the operating system hands to every program; in Python `os.environ` is a dict of them. The example below turns the ones starting with `APP_` into one layer.

Writes, updates and deletes affect only the **first** dict (`maps[0]`). That makes layers easy: `child = config.new_child()` puts a new empty dict at the front, so assignments to `child` never touch the layers behind it, and `child.parents` gives the chain without that front dict. Python looks up variable names the same way: first inside the current function, then in the enclosing code, then the built-ins.

`cm.maps` is the list of dicts in the chain, which you can inspect or change.

Gotchas:

- Deleting a key that exists only in a later dict raises `KeyError`, since deletes only touch the first one.
- `len()` and looping work out the combined keys of all the dicts, which takes time for big ones.
- For a one-off merge, `d1 | d2` (Python 3.9+) is simpler and gives an ordinary dict.
concepts.code:
import os
from collections import ChainMap

defaults = {"host": "localhost", "port": 8000, "debug": False}
file_cfg = {"port": 9000}
env_cfg = {k[4:].lower(): v for k, v in os.environ.items() if k.startswith("APP_")}
cli = {"debug": True}

config = ChainMap(cli, env_cfg, file_cfg, defaults)
print(config["port"], config["debug"], config["host"])   # 9000 True localhost

file_cfg["host"] = "db.internal"                         # changes show through
print(config["host"])                                    # db.internal

scope = config.new_child()
scope["port"] = 1234                                     # written to the new layer
print(scope["port"], config["port"])                     # 1234 9000
print(dict(scope.parents) == dict(config))               # True
print(sorted(config))      # ['debug', 'host', 'port']
takeaways: ChainMap searches several dicts in order without copying them
Writes and deletes affect only the first dict
`new_child()` adds a new front layer; `parents` drops it
pitfalls: Expecting `del chain[key]` to remove a key that lives in a later mapping.

quiz.q: cm = ChainMap({}, {'a': 1}); cm['a'] = 2. What does the second dict contain afterwards?
quiz.explain: Assignments go to maps[0], so the first dict gets 'a': 2 and the second is untouched.

concepts.name: namedtuple vs NamedTuple vs dataclass
concepts.summary: Choose between collections.namedtuple, typing.NamedTuple and dataclasses for record types, knowing the trade-offs.
concepts.why: Picking the right record type decides whether it can change, how much memory it uses, whether it has types, and how safely you can extend it later.
concepts.body:
Three ways to define a record:

- `collections.namedtuple("P", "x y")`: built by a function call, no types, and a real tuple.
- `typing.NamedTuple` written as a class: the same kind of tuple, plus type annotations, defaults and methods:

```python
class P(NamedTuple):
    x: int
    y: int = 0
```

- `@dataclass` classes: ordinary classes whose `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` are written for you; changeable unless `frozen=True`. Options include `slots=True` (store fields in fixed slots instead of a per-object dict, saving memory), `order=True` (allow `<` comparisons) and `kw_only=True` (fields must be passed by name).

Trade-offs:

- **Tuple behaviour** is a feature and a risk. Named tuples unpack, index and compare equal to plain tuples: `P(1, 2) == (1, 2)`. A dataclass compares equal only to objects of the same class. Adding a field to a named tuple breaks every caller that unpacks it as `x, y = p`.
- **Changeability**: named tuples can never change; dataclasses let you choose.
- **Memory**: named tuples are as compact as tuples; dataclasses with `slots=True` come close.
- **Checks and computed fields**: dataclasses run `__post_init__` right after setting the fields, a natural place to check values or compute extra ones. Named tuples can't customise `__init__`, so there's no simple place for checks.

Rule of thumb: use NamedTuple when the record genuinely is a tuple (results that callers unpack, lines of a CSV file, coordinates), and dataclasses for the main objects of your program that may grow new fields.
concepts.code:
from collections import namedtuple
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import NamedTuple

PointA = namedtuple("PointA", "x y")

class PointB(NamedTuple):
    x: int
    y: int = 0
    def norm2(self):
        return self.x ** 2 + self.y ** 2

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class PointC:
    x: int
    y: int = 0

print(PointA(1, 2) == (1, 2), PointB(1, 2) == (1, 2))   # True True
print(PointC(1, 2) == (1, 2))                          # False
print(PointB(3, 4).norm2(), PointB(5))                 # 25 PointB(x=5, y=0)
x, y = PointB(7, 8)                                    # unpacking works
print(PointB.__annotations__)          # {'x': <class 'int'>, 'y': <class 'int'>}
print(isinstance(PointB(1), tuple), isinstance(PointC(1), tuple))  # True False
takeaways: namedtuple and typing.NamedTuple both create real tuples; NamedTuple adds types and methods
Tuple equality and unpacking make named tuples hard to extend later
Use dataclasses for objects that may grow; NamedTuple for genuinely tuple-like data
pitfalls: Returning a NamedTuple from code other people call, then being unable to add a field without breaking callers that unpack it.

quiz.q: Which record type compares equal to a plain tuple with the same values?
options: A plain class with x and y attributes
quiz.explain: NamedTuple instances are tuples, so tuple equality applies.

concepts.name: collections.abc: container interfaces
concepts.summary: Use the abstract base classes in collections.abc to check what an object can do, and to build full dict-like or list-like types from a few methods.
concepts.why: Code written against general kinds like Mapping or Iterable accepts many types, and inheriting from them saves you writing dozens of methods.
concepts.body:
`collections.abc` holds the **ABCs** (abstract base classes) behind Python's built-in collections. Each one describes a kind of object by the methods it must have: `Iterable` (anything a `for` loop can go through), `Sized` (has a length), `Container` (supports `in`), `Sequence` (list-like), `MutableSequence`, `Set`, `Mapping` (dict-like, read only), `MutableMapping`, plus `Callable`, `Hashable` and others.

Two uses:

**Checking what an object can do.** `isinstance(x, Mapping)` is true for dicts, OrderedDicts, ChainMaps and other dict-like classes, which is better than `isinstance(x, dict)`. Simple ABCs like `Iterable` and `Sized` judge a class only by its methods: any class with an `__iter__` method counts as `Iterable` without inheriting from it.

The same names work in type hints, the notes saying what type a parameter should be. Use the most general one you need, such as `Iterable[str]` or `Mapping[str, int]`, so callers can pass any fitting type. Since Python 3.9 the square brackets work directly on the `collections.abc` names.

**Getting methods for free.** Inherit from an ABC and write its few **abstract methods**, the ones it names but doesn't supply. The ABC then fills in the rest as mixin methods. For `Mapping` you write `__getitem__`, `__iter__` and `__len__`, and receive `get`, `keys`, `items`, `values`, `__contains__` and `__eq__`. `MutableMapping` also needs `__setitem__` and `__delitem__` and gives you `pop`, `update`, `setdefault` and more. Forget an abstract method and creating an object fails with `TypeError`, listing what's missing.

The documentation's table of ABCs lists the abstract and mixin methods of each; it's worth bookmarking.
takeaways: Check `isinstance(x, Mapping)` rather than `dict` to accept every dict-like type
Inherit an ABC and write its abstract methods to get the other methods free
In type hints, use the most general ABC you need
pitfalls: Subclassing an ABC but missing one abstract method; instantiation then raises TypeError.

quiz.q: To build a read-only mapping by inheriting collections.abc.Mapping, which methods must you implement?
quiz.explain: Mapping's abstract methods are __getitem__, __iter__ and __len__; the rest are mixins.

concepts.name: Subclassing dict vs UserDict
concepts.summary: Understand why overriding methods on a dict subclass is unreliable, and when to use UserDict, MutableMapping or __missing__ instead.
concepts.why: Custom dictionaries that silently skip your checks are a common, hard-to-spot bug.
concepts.body:
Subclassing `dict` directly looks natural, but dict's built-in methods are written in C inside the interpreter and **don't call your overrides**. If you override `__setitem__` to tidy up keys, then `dict.update()`, creating the dict with `dict(...)`, `setdefault()` and `|=` all skip it. Likewise, overriding `__getitem__` doesn't change `get()`.

Options:

- **collections.UserDict** keeps a real dict in `self.data`, and its methods are written in Python on top of your `__getitem__`, `__setitem__` and `__delitem__`. Override those three and everything else (`update`, creating it, `setdefault`) goes through them. The cost is some speed.
- **collections.abc.MutableMapping** gives the same consistency with storage you choose, as in the collections.abc lesson.
- **A dict subclass with `__missing__`**: when a key is absent, dict's `__getitem__` calls `self.__missing__(key)`. That hook *is* honoured, and it's how `defaultdict` and `Counter` work. Note that `get()` doesn't call `__missing__`.

`UserList` and `UserString` play the same role for lists and strings.

Subclassing `dict` is still fine when you only add new methods or `__missing__`, and when speed matters. When you change how existing operations behave, use UserDict or MutableMapping.
takeaways: Built-in dict methods don't call your overridden `__setitem__`/`__getitem__`
UserDict and MutableMapping route every operation through your methods
`__missing__` is honoured by `d[key]` but not by `get`
pitfalls: Overriding `__setitem__` on a dict subclass to check values and assuming `update()` uses it.

quiz.q: class D(dict): def __setitem__(self, k, v): super().__setitem__(k, v * 2). What is D(a=1)['a']?
quiz.explain: dict's built-in creation code stores items directly, without calling the overridden __setitem__.

concepts.name: How deque, Counter and dicts are implemented
concepts.summary: Know how deque, Counter, defaultdict and OrderedDict are built inside, and how fast each operation is, to predict performance.
concepts.why: Choosing the right collection for millions of operations depends on how it is really built, not just on the methods it offers.
concepts.body:
These notes describe **CPython**, the standard Python interpreter, written in C.

**deque** is a **doubly linked list** of fixed-size blocks: each block holds 64 items plus a **pointer** (the memory address) of the block before it and the one after it. Adding or removing at either end is O(1) and rarely needs new memory. Reaching `d[i]` walks block by block from the nearer end, so the middle is O(n), and so are `insert` and `del` in the middle. You can't cut out a section like `d[2:5]`. Memory per item is close to a list's.

**dict** (and so Counter and defaultdict) is a **hash table**: a compact **array** (a row of slots side by side in memory) of entries in the order they were added, plus a separate sparse table of positions found from each key's hash. Lookups, inserts and deletes are O(1) on average. A delete leaves a placeholder entry until the table is next resized, which is why order survives deletes cheaply.

**Counter** is a kind of dict written in Python, but counting from a list uses a helper written in C (`_count_elements`), so `Counter(items)` is much faster than a Python loop. `most_common(n)` uses `heapq.nlargest`, a partial sort that costs O(N log n) for N items; without `n` it sorts everything.

**defaultdict** is a kind of dict written in C that supplies `__missing__`; it costs extra only when a key is missing.

**OrderedDict** is written in C with an extra linked list running through its entries, so `move_to_end` and `popitem(last=False)` are O(1), at the cost of clearly more memory than a plain dict.

**namedtuple** reads a field by name through a small accessor written in C (`_tuplegetter`): slightly slower than `p[0]` but much faster than a dict lookup.
concepts.code:
import sys
import timeit
from collections import Counter, OrderedDict, deque

n = 100_000
lst, dq = list(range(n)), deque(range(n))
t_list = timeit.timeit(lambda: lst.insert(0, lst.pop()), number=2000)
t_deque = timeit.timeit(lambda: dq.appendleft(dq.pop()), number=2000)
print(t_deque < t_list)          # True: O(1) vs O(n) at the left end

t_mid_list = timeit.timeit(lambda: lst[n // 2], number=20000)
t_mid_deque = timeit.timeit(lambda: dq[n // 2], number=20000)
print(t_mid_list < t_mid_deque)  # True: deque indexing walks blocks

words = ["a", "b", "c"] * 50_000
def manual():
    c = {}
    for w in words:
        c[w] = c.get(w, 0) + 1
    return c
print(timeit.timeit(lambda: Counter(words), number=5) < timeit.timeit(manual, number=5))  # True

d, od = dict.fromkeys(range(1000)), OrderedDict.fromkeys(range(1000))
print(sys.getsizeof(od) > sys.getsizeof(d))   # True
takeaways: deque is a linked list of blocks: O(1) at the ends, O(n) in the middle
Counter counts with a C helper; `most_common(n)` uses a partial sort
OrderedDict trades extra memory for O(1) reordering
pitfalls: Reading a deque by position in a loop that runs millions of times; use a list for that.

quiz.q: Which operation is O(n) on a deque of n items?
quiz.explain: Indexing in the middle has to walk through the linked blocks from the nearer end.

concepts.name: Containers and thread safety
concepts.summary: Which deque and dict operations are safe between threads, why Counter increments can be lost, and what changes in free-threaded Python 3.13.
concepts.why: Sharing collections between threads without knowing which steps can be interrupted leads to rare, data-corrupting bugs.
concepts.body:
An operation is **atomic** when it happens as one indivisible step: another thread can never see it half-done. Thread safety in CPython comes down to which operations are atomic.

**Single operations.** `deque.append`, `appendleft`, `pop` and `popleft` are documented as thread-safe, so a deque can carry items between threads without a lock. Single dict operations such as `d[k] = v`, `d.get(k)` and `d.pop(k, None)` are effectively atomic as well. In the normal build the GIL provides this. The optional **free-threaded build** of 3.13 (`python3.13t`) has no GIL, so threads truly run at once; it keeps these guarantees with small internal locks on each object.

**Combined operations** are never atomic. `counter[key] += 1` is a read, an add and a write; two threads can read the same old value, and one increment is lost. The same applies to `if key not in d: d[key] = ...`, defaultdict factories that do real work, and looping over a dict while another thread changes it (`RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`).

Approaches:

- Protect combined updates with a `threading.Lock`: only one thread at a time can be inside `with lock:`.
- Use `queue.Queue` to hand work from one thread to another; its `get` waits until an item arrives, and `task_done` tracks finished work.
- Give each thread its own Counter and merge them at the end with `+=` or `update`, which needs no lock at all.
- `d.setdefault(k, v)` is a single operation, useful for "insert if absent".

Free-threading makes races that were rare under the GIL much more frequent, so code that relied on luck breaks quickly.
takeaways: deque append/pop operations are thread-safe; single dict operations are atomic
`counter[k] += 1` is read, add, write and can lose updates without a lock
Count per thread and merge, or use a lock or `queue.Queue`
pitfalls: Assuming the GIL makes `+=` on shared counters safe; increments can be lost, especially on free-threaded builds.

quiz.q: Four threads each run counts['k'] += 1 one million times on a shared Counter without a lock. What final value is guaranteed?
quiz.explain: The increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so concurrent updates can be lost.
